title: There is no point in trying to finish my old projects without AI.
author: FutureLynx_
selftext:
These are games started in Unreal Engine some with Blueprints. And blueprints dont work well with AI.

I shelved them and started making a new project purely with HTML and JS, and im getting more progress in 3 days than i got in 3 weeks.

Im also questioning at what point are these engines worth it and if the editors just get in the way.

My old projects are shelved precisely because of this.

I'm betting on the possibility that AI will be able to complete them in days in the future.

At the moment since they use blueprints quite a lot, it is still not very reliable, and prone to mistakes that can take hours and constant closing, compile, reopening of the editor.

I think very soon AI will be able to convert all Blueprint code to C++ elegantly and fast.

Only then I will complete those projects.

Right now it is not worth it to try to work my way through blueprints, and the C++. Its better to prototype ideas in JS and HTML fast.

If these ideas work I can then convert them to Godot or even Unreal later.

Anyone feels the same?

comments.author: StretchedNut
comments.body: Similar experience. I’ve been a game dev since before AI. One of my games I released last year was made with 99% hand coded stuff, and since then I’ve been using AI a lot more. That game needed an update, and it pained me to go into it and use all my old systems and way of working after being so use to the advantages that AI gave me on my new projects.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: I found myself reanimating old projects and having AI review them. It's crazy how it finds old bugs and immediately fixes them. Stuff like "when you go back to the title screen the Continue button has no text". Takes a while to figure that one out, but Codex immediately cross references everything.

comments.author: Funnyman1217
comments.body:
The next big realization around AI is the fact that everyone will produce the same generic games and experiences as everyone else. Look at what AI has done to webpage design. They all look the exact same. That is the point with AI, it is very good at applying process and patterns to meet demands. It sucks balls at deciding if something is fun or playable.

BUT you should never stop there unless that is what you are satisfied with. To break out of the crowed you will need to add your own personal touch to make it stand out. 

AI cant do that for you. You just need to adjust your demands and expectations of yourself and get real about what you want and can do.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
AI is there for ease of execution. Tying up loose ends. Running automated tests. It still needs constraints, a container, architectural design.

If you ask it to do everything it is going to build a generic AI looking thing.

If you design how you want things to behave and outline the cases, it is a wonderfully efficient executor.

Essentially with AI we are being pushed to a higher level of management. 

If you are a project manager and all you tell your team is “I want to do A.” You’re not going to get good results either

replies.author: Itchy-Individual3536
replies.body: Yeah, we had website builders before AI, and web frameworks with templates that everyone could use more or less easily to build a website that looked professional, but at the same time pretty generic. And it was soemtimes hard or impossible to break out of the framework you were given, using or developing own plugins etc. - think Wordpress or Bootstrap. AI now makes everything go a step forward in professional look and feel, even the easiest things, and makes it possible to smoothly grow out of the very easy, very generic frame into the realm of using you own creative ideas and designs if you just explain them well enough, making it a product you "own" at some point even though it was executed by AI - then AI becomes the tool which just replaces or sits on top of other tools which we also don't see as "not making it yourself", like a find&replace function, code completion, image editing software, using a Unity library, or a compiler.

replies.author: 12redandblack12
replies.body: true. here's the thing with passion projects from my experience, not just game dev, and why most of the time they get shelved. you start with a really cool idea, and it's initially fun and exciting... but then you hit a rough patch where executing it becomes hard work, tedious and time consuming. your fun little side hobby starts to feel like a second job. ai is good for helping your through that patch.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
Agreed. TBH solo devs have always had an IMPOSSIBLE task. To be architect visionary  project manager, systems designer, coder, QA. You’re a company in one person. The success stories are so minimal and fantastic. 

AI takes half that equation away. If you are a good architect and designer and project manager, you can now reasonably do away with the execution somewhat.

But with AI I think the bar will also be raised. Execution becomes so much less time consuming that the market will eventually demand higher quality product. It will become harder again to stand out from the rest. As it should be

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
I barely use the editor in Unity, but I don't use Unity for the editor. Having an engine is useful for a few things still, but those things are huge asks otherwise:

1. Physics. Yes you can build your own physics system in a custom engine, but if you've tried building our full systems like this you'll understand just how many pitfalls and bugs you run into. It will work eventually, and probably be pretty great, but you'll constantly be tuning it for optimizations, adding features, debugging those features, optimizing further, etc. You will be reinventing a wheel that will take weeks at minimum and more likely months or years (depending on how much time you actually invest into it) of development time away from your game. If you have very specific needs this may be necessary (Noita, for example, needed custom particle and physics systems to handle what it wanted to do.) and is just part of your game's development. But if you don't need something crazy, having an established system in place will save you a lot of time and headaches because it 'just works'.

2. Lighting, VFX, Streaming and  Memory Management, etc. Just like with physics, these are all systems you'd have to bake in. Even animation and motion controllers. Every one of these is a large undertaking to put in all the features a game needs (depending on the game, in fairness.)  All of them will generally be riddled with normal bugs you'd have to iterate out and the more of these you have the harder it will be to track down the cause each time.

3. Plugin access. The main engines have a lot of plugins available that you can possibly get for free, or buy for a few bucks. Yes you might be able to AI your way to the same result, but it will be less polished at first and the token costs (even at sub rates) will likely far exceed the cost of just buying the thing. Having these available, even if you don't use them, is handy. It's the same reason I use blender even though I could AI up a Blender based program that would work better for my specific workflow. It'd take oodles of time, I couldn't use powerful plugins that already exist with it, and to actually implement all the features it has would be difficult. AI also has some amount of training and clear documentation for the program (like it does for major game engines) which can help it utilize those tools better than in your own custom one unless you finetune an AI on it.

So yeah. It's really not about the editor. I mean, a clean editor helps for making some manual adjustments to things like your scene placement, settings, assignments, whatever. But those aren't really gamebreakers at all when you're mostly vibe-ing. However make sure to take into account all the other features an engine provides that you'd otherwise be building from scratch (and more importantly - debugging from scratch.)

Also most editors, while annoying to recompile and can increase iterative time in that way, don't actually add bloat to the game itself. There might be some exceptions, like systems that are a bit more complex than they need to be for your game, but I think most engines have options to use simpler forms, or you can probably just build your own custom implementation without tapping into their physics engine for calculations at that point (for instance you don't have to use Nanite or Lumen in your Unreal game, and it won't affect your game's code if you don't.)

comments.author: senseven
comments.body: I have larger ideas that I put to rest, because I didn't know Godot good enough to make them work the way I wanted. Started way smaller projects to learn the engine and do everything the proper way. Ai is a damn good teacher, if you are willing to learn. You can discuss a coarse solution, then let the communication flow into refinement, then implementation. I use the engine the intended way, everything is properly named and so on. I can work a couple of hours on one specific idea and then forget about it for a while. It never becomes "messy" that I don't want to touch it. People one shotting ideas change manual hacking with vibing. The result is the same, you don't want to touch it three month later.
